Our own team 24 builds it. So do outside contributors who earn the access. 25 26 Note-taking, design tooling, knowledge management: categories most people 27 treat as solved. We keep finding the part incumbents leave broken, and 28 ship the fix as a real, running product. 29 30 ## Products 31 32 ### Chapters 33 A self-hostable knowledge base: markdown notes, a knowledge graph AI 34 agents can query and edit through MCP with full tool parity. Real-time 35 multiplayer editing runs on Yjs, with per-operation permission checks and 36 instant revocation. Hybrid keyword and semantic search runs permission- 37 filtered, in-query. Export is a first-class feature: zip exports, expiring 38 share links, full-instance backup and restore. 39 40 **Why we built it.** Most knowledge tools bolt AI on top, a chat window 41 pointed at your notes after the fact. We wanted AI access built into the 42 data layer itself, so an agent navigates the actual graph instead of 43 guessing from a prompt. That became the single governing criterion for 44 every stack decision that followed: how well it serves AI navigability. 45 46 **How we build it.** TypeScript end to end: one language, one runtime, one 47 deployable unit. Fastify for the API. Yjs and Hocuspocus run the realtime 48 CRDT relay in the same process as the API, because MCP writes need to 49 flow through that relay as first-class participants with per-operation 50 permission checks. Postgres holds accounts, sessions, and the search 51 index; notes stay plain markdown files on disk. Embeddings run locally 52 through Transformers.js, so note content never leaves the instance. We 53 seriously considered a Python/FastAPI backend for its graph and embedding 54 libraries, then rejected it: those advantages are batch-shaped and 55 invisible to an AI reading the graph, and the cost was two runtimes to 56 deploy plus a security-critical CRDT relay rebuilt on a less mature 57 library. The UI is next. 58 → [github.com/PIIIX-org/chapters](https://github.com/PIIIX-org/chapters) 59 60 ### Vectory 61 A canvas you design on that writes real, production-ready HTML and CSS as 62 you build, with a live preview and an inspectable code panel over the 63 output. Built for designers who want to ship a real site without becoming 64 developers, and for developers who want a faster prototyping loop. 65 66 **Why we're investigating it.** The AI design-tool market looks crowded 67 at a glance: Onlook covers canvas UX and AI codegen for React, Anthropic 68 ships its own code-powered prototyping tool on its flagship model, 69 Lovable raised $330M proving how large the category already is. Static 70 marketing-site HTML and CSS, built from a Figma-style canvas as the entry 71 point, was still open. Before writing a line of product code, we ran the 72 research to check whether that gap was real. 73 74 **How we build it.** Research first: a multi-agent research harness ran 75 five parallel search angles across fifteen sources, with every claim 76 adversarially re-verified across three independent passes before it 77 counted as fact. Twelve architecture diagrams map the full system ahead 78 of implementation: the client/server split, the codegen pipeline, the 79 data model, real-time sync. The plan underneath it: a designer places 80 shapes, text, and images on a canvas, and an LLM turns that canvas state 81 into semantic, exportable HTML and CSS as they work, with a live preview 82 pane that keeps the generated code visible and editable throughout. 83 84 Currently in the architecture and competitive-research stage. 85 → [github.com/PIIIX-org/vectory](https://github.com/PIIIX-org/vectory) 86 87 ### Yildizim 88 A closed-source, gamified 3D visualization layer for hosted Chapters: a 89 galaxy where every star is a note, built so a personal knowledge graph 90 feels explorable. Shipped and running today, inside Chapters. 91 92 **Why we built it.** A knowledge graph with hundreds of thousands of 93 notes is hard to browse as a list or a flat map. We wanted exploring your 94 own notes to feel like discovery: a 3D space you fly through, gamified 95 enough that returning to your own knowledge base is something you want 96 to do, not a chore. 97 98 **How we build it.** A real-time 3D renderer holding 60 frames per second 99 at 371,000 notes. Development runs in research-backed phases rather than 100 one large redesign: audio, color palette, camera rotation, depth of 101 field, minimap, polish, each phase shipped and merged as its own reviewed 102 pull request. 37 pull requests in, and running live inside Chapters 103 today. 104 105 ## How we're organized 106 107 Every role maps to real GitHub access, not a title: 108 109 | Role | Access | What they do | 110 |---|---|---| 111 | Manager | Maintain | Repo settings, branch protection, merges | 112 | Developer | Write | Pushes code, opens and merges pull requests | 113 | Reviewer | Triage | Reviews pull requests, triages issues | 114 | Designer | Write | Pushes UI and asset pull requests | 115 | Docs/Content | Write | Pushes docs and README changes | 116 | Community/Support | Triage | Labels and triages issues, helps other contributors | 117 118 These roles aren't handed out at the start. A contributor forks the repo, 119 opens a pull request, and earns a role from there. 120 121 ## How we work 122 123 Fork a repo. Open a pull request. Sign the CLA in a comment on that PR. 124 Contribute well and you earn write access, with the exact bar for each 125 role spelled out in 126 [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/PIIIX-org/.github/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md). 127 A pull request doesn't merge without a passing CLA check. 128 129 ## Hiring and partnerships 130 131 Look at Chapters and Vectory directly before you take our word for 132 anything. The architecture choices and the commit history say what this 133 team can do. 134 135

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances.
